summary: First English narrative for Intel's 1985 decision to leave DRAMs, written from the case's primary-source facts (Intel 1984-1987 annual reports; Grove's account; Burgelman 1994).

narrative.hook: It is 1985, the memory-chip market has collapsed, and the company that invented the business is now a minor player in it. You and your chairman have to decide whether to keep fighting for memory, or walk away from the product your company was built on.
narrative.short_setup: Intel came out of 1984 with record revenue of about $1.63 billion and net income of about $198 million. It had raised capital spending by 168 percent to $388 million, and only that year it had announced the world's first 256K CHMOS dynamic RAM. Then the boom ended. In the last quarter of 1984 the computer industry went into a slump just as new chip capacity came on stream around the world. Through 1985 customers worked off their inventories, prices fell precipitously, and Intel's new orders hit bottom in the second quarter, when the company began losing money on its operations. In DRAMs, the business Intel was founded on, it had become a minor participant in a crowded market that Asian and other non-U.S. manufacturers were targeting. Its microprocessors, by contrast, had become the standard for personal computers, and a 32-bit successor, the 80386, was in development. Andrew Grove, the president, and Gordon Moore, the chairman, had to decide what Intel was.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: Staying in DRAMs was not sentimentality. The slump was hitting the whole semiconductor industry, not only memory, and a company that leaves a market at the bottom of a cycle can find it has abandoned that market just before the recovery. Intel was not standing still technically: in 1984 it had announced the first 256K DRAM built in CHMOS, a technology its annual report said many expected to become mainstream for DRAMs later in the decade. A high-volume memory line is also the kind of product Intel itself relied on to refine its manufacturing techniques. And DRAM was what Intel had been founded to make. Walking away meant closing plants, laying people off, and conceding a market to foreign rivals.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: The case for leaving was that Intel no longer had a position worth defending. By its executives' own account, DRAM had been targeted by non-U.S. manufacturers to the point where it was difficult to earn a return on the investment required just to participate, and Intel had become a minor player. Every dollar and every wafer start spent fighting for a commodity it could not win was a dollar and a wafer start withheld from microprocessors, where Intel set the standard for the personal computer and where demand had outrun supply as recently as 1984. With the industry in a slump and money scarce, spreading resources across both looked like a way to lose in both. Intel could keep its EPROM line, a memory product it had invented and still led, as the volume product for developing manufacturing processes.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: Grove later described the moment the question was settled. In the middle of 1985 he asked Moore: 'If we got kicked out and the board brought in a new CEO, what do you think he would do?' Moore answered without hesitation: 'He would get us out of memories.' Grove, by his own account, stared at him numb, then said: 'Why shouldn't you and I walk out the door, come back, and do it ourselves?' Intel announced the exit to its employees on 10 October 1985. The executives' explanation in the 1985 annual report was blunt: DRAM had been targeted by non-U.S. manufacturers, so it was difficult to produce a return on the investment required. Grove would later call it 'an emotional decision.' Intel kept EPROMs and put its weight behind microprocessors.
narrative.outcome_story: The same month as the announcement, Intel unveiled the 80386, which worked to full-speed specification on its first manufacturing run. But the downturn had further to go. Intel's net income for 1985 was about $1.6 million on revenue down 16 percent. In 1986 it decided to sell its bubble memory business, took a $60 million restructuring charge, and lost about $173 million. Over 1985-86 it closed eight older plants and cut 7,200 jobs through attrition and layoffs. Then, in 1987, revenue rose 51 percent and net income reached a record $248 million. The annual report credited a new generation of desktop computers built around Intel's advanced microprocessors.
narrative.hindsight_analysis:
This is a case where the decision and the outcome were both good, which makes it easy to forget that one does not prove the other. Judge the decision on what Grove and Moore had in 1985. Intel was a minor participant in a market that better-funded competitors were targeting, the slump had removed any margin for a sub-scale player, and the company's distinctive position was in microprocessors, where it was the standard and had a new generation coming. Keeping EPROMs protected the part of memory that mattered for process technology. On that evidence, leaving was the stronger choice, and the argument for staying, that the market might recover, did not answer the question of whether Intel could ever win it back.

The weaker part is timing. Robert Burgelman's 1994 study found that Intel's internal allocation of scarce manufacturing capacity had already shifted from memory to microprocessors before corporate strategy was officially changed. Through the company's internal process for deciding where capacity went, resources had been moving away from DRAMs while the official strategy still treated Intel as a memory company. On that reading, the famous conversation ratified a shift the organization had already made. The decision was right in direction and late in arriving.

The outcome also involved things outside the decision. The 1987 recovery depended on personal computer makers building a new generation of machines around the 80386, which Intel could hope for but not guarantee. And the 1986 loss and the 7,200 jobs cut were driven largely by the industry-wide collapse, which would have hurt Intel whether it stayed in DRAMs or not. Grove's verdict that this was 'the best business decision we ever made' is a participant's judgment made with full knowledge of how things turned out. The better lesson is that the decision was sound before anyone knew the ending.
narrative.decision_principle: When a business you are attached to has become one you would never enter today, ask what a newcomer with no history would do, and check whether your organization's own resource choices have already answered the question for you.
narrative.longform_story:
In the middle of 1985, Andrew Grove asked Gordon Moore a question. At the time Moore was Intel's chairman and chief executive, and Grove its president. Grove, by his own later account, asked: 'If we got kicked out and the board brought in a new CEO, what do you think he would do?' Moore answered without hesitation. 'He would get us out of memories.' Grove stared at him, numb. Then he said: 'Why shouldn't you and I walk out the door, come back, and do it ourselves?'

The question was hard because of what memories meant to Intel. Memory chips were the business the company had been founded on. As recently as 1984 Intel had announced the world's first 256K dynamic RAM built in CHMOS, a technology its annual report said many people expected to become the mainstream way of making DRAMs later in the decade. A year before, the company had been talking about the future of its memory business, not its end.

The year 1984 had been the best in Intel's history. Revenue reached about $1.63 billion and net income about $198 million. Demand for semiconductors was so intense, fuelled by the spread of the personal computer, that customers could not get enough of them, especially Intel's microprocessors. Intel raised its capital spending by 168 percent, to $388 million, and licensed other manufacturers to produce its microprocessors so that customers would feel assured of supply.

Then, in the last quarter of 1984, the boom collapsed. The computer industry went into a slump at the moment large amounts of new chip capacity came on stream around the world. Customers who had ordered heavily found themselves with too much inventory. Prices fell precipitously. Intel's new orders reached their lowest point in the second quarter of 1985, and the company slid into operating losses.

The slump hit everything, but it exposed memory most. In DRAMs, Intel had become a minor participant in a crowded market. Its executives later wrote that the business had been targeted by non-U.S. manufacturers, so that it was difficult to produce a return on the investment needed simply to compete, and that Asian-based rivals had forced Intel to focus on manufacturing technology just to stay in the game. In microprocessors the picture was the reverse. Intel's chips had become the standard for personal computers. In 1984 production of the 80186 had tripled every quarter and still not kept up with demand. And a new 32-bit chip, the 80386, was in development.

There was a real argument for staying. The downturn was industry-wide, and leaving at the bottom of a cycle could mean abandoning a market just before it recovered. Intel had invested in new memory technology and had the engineers to keep improving it. High-volume memory lines were the kind of product Intel used to refine its manufacturing processes. And quitting meant plant closures and layoffs, and handing a market to foreign competitors.

But the argument for leaving went to the root of the problem. Intel was not a temporary casualty of a bad year in DRAMs; it was a small player in a commodity market against rivals determined to win it. Every wafer start spent there was one not spent on microprocessors, where Intel led. And there was a way to keep what memory gave the company technically: Intel could stay in EPROMs, the erasable memory chips it had invented in 1971 and led in every generation since, and use them as the volume product for developing manufacturing processes.

On 10 October 1985 Intel announced to its employees that it was leaving the DRAM business. Grove would later call it 'an emotional decision,' noting that Intel had been the first to introduce the product and build the business. In the annual report for 1985, he and Moore put it in a sentence: the market had been targeted by non-U.S. manufacturers, so it was difficult to produce a return on the investment required to be a participant.

That same month Intel unveiled the 80386. It contained some 275,000 transistors and worked at full speed on the first manufacturing run. The annual report called it the most complete and most favourably received microprocessor announcement in Intel's history, and customers began committing system designs to it.

The recovery did not come quickly. Intel's net income for 1985 was about $1.6 million, on revenue down 16 percent. In 1986 the company decided to sell its bubble memory business too, took a $60 million restructuring charge, and lost about $173 million. Over two years it closed eight older plants and reduced its workforce by 7,200 people through attrition and layoffs. Grove and Moore wrote that Intel had been left with an overhead structure built for the $2-3 billion company it had wanted to be, rather than the $1.0-1.5 billion company it was becoming.

In 1987 the picture turned. Revenue rose 51 percent and net income reached $248 million, a record. The annual report explained why: during the bad years, customers had been busy designing new computers around Intel's advanced microprocessors, and in 1987 those machines reached the market.

There is a second version of this story. In 1994 the Stanford scholar Robert Burgelman published a study of how Intel actually left the memory business. He found that Intel's internal process for allocating scarce manufacturing capacity had already shifted resources from memory to microprocessors before the official strategy changed. While the company's official strategy still treated Intel as a memory company, actions taken by middle-level managers had been moving manufacturing resources toward microprocessors. On Burgelman's reading, the conversation between Grove and Moore did not start the change; it caught up with it.

Both versions can be true. The decision to leave was sound on the evidence of 1985, and it would have been sound even if the 80386 had stumbled. It was also late: the organization had seen the answer before its leaders said it aloud. Grove called it the best business decision Intel ever made. The more useful observation is that it was a good decision before anyone knew how it would end.
